explanations.explanation: Yes, the Herodians, supporters of King Herod's family, walk up right alongside the Pharisees' disciples. The text says the Pharisees sent their disciples to Him "along with the Herodians." So the Pharisees stay back and let others deliver the question. I'd call that a plan with a very safe seat in the back.

The Samaritans, a people from the region of Samaria, never show up in this passage. The Pharisees send their disciples "along with the Herodians." That's the whole guest list for this little visit. Nobody from Samaria got the invite, or the group text.

The Levites, men from the tribe of Levi, aren't part of this scene. The text says the Pharisees sent their disciples "along with the Herodians." Those are the only two groups mentioned. I know it feels like a crowd, but it's a small crowd.

It's actually the opposite. They say, "…You pay no attention to external appearance." In other words, they say Jesus doesn't judge by how someone looks. They're stacking the compliments pretty high at this point. I'd be checking my pockets by now.

Right, because the text says the opposite. They tell Jesus, "You seek favor from no one, because You pay no attention to external appearance." That's another compliment in the pile. Honestly, they're buttering Him up like a fresh tray of cookies, and the tray keeps coming.

Yes, taxes. They ask, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?" Caesar was the Roman emperor, so this question was about paying money to the ruler of Rome. It's a yes-or-no question, and I think they hoped either answer would get Jesus in trouble. That part is my guess, baker, but the text does say they wanted to trap Him in His words.

That's not the word they use. They ask whether it's lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. Caesar was the Roman emperor, so this is about paying the ruler, not a gift for something else. It's a close guess, but the real word is taxes.

Not wages, though I'd love a question about my wages sometime. They ask, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?" Caesar was the Roman emperor, and they're asking about money going to him. Nobody in this scene is getting paid anything.

That's it. Jesus says, "You hypocrites, why are you testing Me?" The text tells us He knew their evil intent. All those sweet words were sitting on top of something else. And He names it right away, with no wind-up.
Jesus doesn't call them thieves here. He says, "You hypocrites, why are you testing Me?" The text says He knew their evil intent. They came with nice words, and He answers what was really going on.

Not strangers. Jesus says, "You hypocrites, why are you testing Me?" The text says He knew their evil intent. They came in like old friends with all those compliments, but Jesus wasn't fooled for a second.

Yes, the same men who came to test Him. Jesus says, "Show Me the coin used for the tax," and the text says, "they brought Him a denarius." Think about that for a second. The coin comes out of their own pockets. I think that's the funniest part of the whole scene, but that's just me.

Simon Peter, one of Jesus' twelve disciples (Matthew 10:2), isn't in this scene at all. The text says the men who came to test Jesus are the ones who "brought Him a denarius." So the coin comes from their side. Good guess on a name you know, though.

Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve disciples (Matthew 10:4), isn't in this passage. After Jesus asks for the coin, the text says "they brought Him a denarius." That "they" is the group who came to test Him. They're the ones holding the coin.
Yes. Jesus asks, "Whose image is this, and whose inscription?" and they answer, "Caesar's." That's a question anyone could answer in one word. And that one word sets up what Jesus says next.

Herod is the king whose family the Herodians support, but he isn't who they name. Asked whose image and inscription are on the coin, they answer, "Caesar's." It's the same Caesar from the question about taxes. The whole conversation stays on him.

Pilate, the Roman governor (Matthew 27:2), isn't named here. When Jesus asks whose image and inscription are on the coin, they answer, "Caesar's." That's the same Caesar they asked about from the start. One name, one coin, and no governor in sight.

Jesus doesn't say that. The text says, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's." So He doesn't tell them to refuse the tax. Look at how He answers, baker. The coin does the talking.

Right. What Jesus actually says is, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's." He never tells them not to pay. He answers the question with the coin they just handed Him, and with one line about Caesar and God.
Yes. The text says, "when they heard this, they were amazed." Then they left Him and went away. They came with a plan and went home with a lot to think about. I'd be amazed too, baker.
The text says the opposite. "When they heard this, they were amazed." After that, they left Him and went away. So amazed is exactly the word, friend.
